issues.legal_issue: A conviction is not vitiated by an omission to put the accused’s alleged individual act to him where the prosecution account disclosed that act and the omission caused no prejudice to his defence.
material_facts: The charge alleged that the accused, as a member of an unlawful assembly, was liable for the murder committed in furtherance of its common object; it did not separately charge him with personally stabbing the deceased.

In his examination under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code, the accused was asked only about the assembly’s alleged acts and was not specifically asked whether he had struck the deceased with a spear.
The first information report and the eyewitness testimony alleged that this accused had delivered the fatal blow.
The accused did not claim in the High Court that the omission had prejudiced his defence; the point was raised for the first time in the Supreme Court.
issues.conclusion: The omission did not prejudice the accused in his trial and did not vitiate the conviction on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: A defect or omission in the charge or in the accused’s examination does not invalidate a trial where, considering the circumstances, the accused was not prejudiced in his defence. The Court applied this principle to the charge and examination under Section 342 of the Criminal Procedure Code; it cited no earlier case on this point.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and charge_omitted_individual_act and examination_omitted_individual_act and prosecution_evidence_disclosed_individual_act and no_defence_prejudice_shown

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by a person convicted at trial.
predicates.charge_omitted_individual_act: The charge alleged group liability but did not separately state the accused’s alleged individual act.
predicates.examination_omitted_individual_act: The accused was not specifically asked during examination about the alleged individual act.
predicates.prosecution_evidence_disclosed_individua: The prosecution’s report or witness testimony described the accused as committing the individual act.
predicates.no_defence_prejudice_shown: The accused did not show that the omission impaired the ability to defend against the allegation.

issues.definition: When a convicted person appeals, an omitted individual act in the charge and examination does not vitiate the trial if the prosecution evidence disclosed the act and no defence prejudice was shown.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution account is insufficient to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt when unexplained delay in forwarding the first information report, material differences between that report and the trial account, and the withholding of material witnesses collectively undermine the reliability of the evidence.
material_facts: The first information report was recorded as having been lodged in the morning, but it was sent to the Magistrate the following day and received about two days after the stated lodging time; no explanation was offered for the delay.

The report described the accused as arriving without invitation and beginning the assault, while the informant testified that he had invited people to his house to settle the dispute and had sent a person to call one of the accused.
The report did not mention that two prosecution witnesses used sticks in their defence or that some accused persons were injured, although those matters were stated in court.

Several people named as eyewitnesses in the report were not examined, including a person who, according to the informant, had been sent to call the accused and was himself injured, and a witness described as independent.
The High Court excluded one claimed eyewitness as unreliable, although the other examined eyewitnesses and the first information report also placed that witness at the scene.
issues.conclusion: The evidence could not be accepted at face value, and the case against the appellants was not proved beyond reasonable doubt; their convictions were set aside and they were directed to be released.
issues.legal_principle: Section 157 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1898 and the corresponding provision of the 1973 Code require the first information report to be sent forthwith to the Magistrate. An unexplained delay may provide a basis to suspect later recording or embellishment, particularly where the trial account materially differs from the report. The Court relied on Mitter Sain v. State of U.P. for the proposition that eyewitness evidence in such circumstances cannot be accepted at face value, and applied the principle that witnesses essential to unfolding the prosecution narrative should be examined.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_conviction and unexplained_fir_forwarding_delay and material_report_trial_discrepancies and material_witnesses_withheld and eyewitness_reliability_weakened

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal by persons convicted at trial.
predicates.unexplained_fir_forwarding_delay: The first information report reached the competent judicial officer substantially later than its stated recording, without an explanation.
predicates.material_report_trial_discrepancies: The trial account differed from the first information report on important features of how the incident began or how participants acted.
predicates.material_witnesses_withheld: The prosecution did not examine witnesses who could materially explain or corroborate its account, without explaining their absence.
predicates.eyewitness_reliability_weakened: The circumstances materially undermined the reliability of the eyewitness account presented by the prosecution.

issues.definition: In an appeal from conviction, unexplained delay, material inconsistencies, withheld material witnesses, and weakened eyewitness reliability together mean that the prosecution has not proved its case beyond reasonable doubt.

issues.legal_issue: Group-liability and rioting convictions cannot stand where the evidence does not establish that the accused were the aggressors and does not prove the individual assaults attributed to them.
material_facts: The prosecution and defence accounts differed about how the fight began, and the Court could not determine with certainty that the accused were the aggressors.
Injuries were sustained by persons on both sides, including two accused persons; one accused had a fractured kneecap and another had multiple injuries.
The Court considered that a free fight had occurred, while finding that the defence account might not itself be wholly true.
The convictions of four accused for grievous hurt, hurt, and assault-related offences were based on group liability, and the prosecution evidence did not establish their individual assaults.
issues.conclusion: The convictions of the four accused under Sections 326, 324, and 323 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code were unsustainable; on the finding that the accused might not have been the aggressors, the convictions under Sections 147 and 148 were also not maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 147 and 148 of the Indian Penal Code could not sustain rioting convictions if the accused were not shown to be the aggressors. Where the evidence instead indicated a free fight and the prosecution did not prove the individual assaults, the convictions for hurt offences founded on Section 149 could not stand.

rule.if: criminal_appeal_from_group_liability_convictions and evidence_indicates_free_fight and aggressor_identity_uncertain and individual_assaults_unproved

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_group_liability_con: The proceeding is an appeal from convictions for offences attributed to an accused group or unlawful assembly.
predicates.evidence_indicates_free_fight: The evidence shows a fight between opposing sides in which persons on both sides were injured.
predicates.aggressor_identity_uncertain: The evidence does not establish which side began the fight or that the accused were the aggressors.
predicates.individual_assaults_unproved: The prosecution does not prove the particular assaults committed by each accused.

issues.definition: In an appeal from group-liability convictions, a free fight, uncertainty about which side was the aggressor, and failure to prove individual assaults mean that the group-liability and rioting convictions cannot stand.

issues.legal_issue: A murder conviction based on eyewitness identification of the assailant cannot stand where the medical evidence does not identify which of two similar seized weapons caused the fatal injury and the weapons were not shown to the medical witness.
material_facts: The deceased died from a sharp punctured wound to the chest, which the medical witness said might have been caused by a spear-like weapon.
The prosecution alleged that one accused used a spear and another used a similar weapon; both types of weapon were seized from their respective houses.
The medical witness had not seen the seized weapons and acknowledged that he could not distinguish between the two types as relevant to the injury.
The eyewitnesses attributed the fatal blow to one accused, but the Court found their evidence could not be accepted without independent corroboration in the circumstances of the case.
issues.conclusion: It could not be determined with certainty whether the fatal injury was caused by the weapon attributed to the convicted accused or by the similar weapon attributed to the other accused; the murder conviction could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: The prosecution, and the Court, should ensure that an alleged weapon of the offence, if available, is shown to the medical witness so that the witness can state whether it could have caused the injuries. Failure to do so may cause a miscarriage of justice. The Court relied on Kartarey v. State of U.P.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_murder_conviction: The proceeding is an appeal from a conviction for murder.
predicates.fatal_injury_could_be_caused_by_similar_: The medical evidence permits the fatal injury to have been caused by either of two similar weapons associated with different people.
predicates.seized_weapons_not_shown_to_medical_witn: The available weapons were not shown to the medical witness for an opinion about which could have caused the injury.
predicates.assailant_attribution_lacks_independent_: The evidence attributing the fatal act to the convicted person lacks independent corroboration sufficient to resolve the uncertainty.

issues.definition: In an appeal from a murder conviction, uncertainty between similar possible weapons, their absence from medical examination, and uncorroborated attribution mean that the murder conviction cannot stand.
